title: Child Development and Pedagogy — Core Batch 02

questions.question: A teacher notices that learners of the same age differ in interests and pace. Which principle is illustrated?
options: Development is uniform for all learners
questions.explanation: Learners develop at different rates and show individual differences in abilities, interests and needs.

questions.question: Which classroom practice best reflects a child-centred approach?
options: Learners explore and discuss ideas actively
All learners copy identical notes silently
questions.explanation: A child-centred classroom gives learners active roles and builds on their needs and experiences.

questions.question: In Piaget’s theory, the ability to reason logically about concrete objects is typical of which stage?
questions.explanation: Concrete operational children can use logical operations with concrete situations.

questions.question: A child uses a schema to interpret a new experience without changing the schema. Piaget called this:
questions.explanation: Assimilation incorporates new information into an existing schema.

questions.question: Changing an existing schema to fit new information is known as:
questions.explanation: Accommodation modifies an existing schema in response to experience.

questions.question: According to Vygotsky, the Zone of Proximal Development refers to tasks a learner can:
options: Complete with appropriate guidance but not yet independently
questions.explanation: The ZPD is the range between independent performance and performance possible with support.

questions.question: Temporary support that is gradually withdrawn as competence grows is called:
questions.explanation: Scaffolding is adjustable support that fades as learners become more capable.

questions.question: Which factor is central to Vygotsky’s account of cognitive development?
questions.explanation: Vygotsky emphasised social interaction, language and culturally developed tools.

questions.question: In Erikson’s psychosocial theory, the major conflict during adolescence is:
questions.explanation: Adolescents work through identity versus role confusion as they form a sense of self.

questions.question: Kohlberg’s theory primarily describes development of:
questions.explanation: Kohlberg proposed stages describing how moral reasoning develops.

questions.question: A learner studies because the topic is interesting and satisfying. This is:
questions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation arises from interest or satisfaction within the activity itself.

questions.question: A reward offered after a desired behaviour is an example of:
questions.explanation: Positive reinforcement adds a consequence that increases the likelihood of a behaviour.

questions.question: In operant conditioning, removing an unpleasant stimulus to strengthen a behaviour is:
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing an aversive condition.

questions.question: Which statement about punishment is most accurate?
options: It always teaches the desired behaviour
It may suppress behaviour but does not necessarily teach an alternative
questions.explanation: Punishment may reduce a behaviour, but learners may still need explicit teaching of an appropriate alternative.

questions.question: A teacher demonstrates a task and learners imitate the model. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Observational learning occurs when people learn by watching and imitating others.

questions.question: Bandura’s concept of self-efficacy refers to a learner’s:
options: Belief in their capability to perform a task
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is a belief about one’s ability to organise and carry out actions for a task.

questions.question: Which is an example of formative assessment?
options: A quick check during a lesson used to adjust teaching
A ranking published after the course
questions.explanation: Formative assessment gathers evidence during learning so teaching and feedback can be adjusted.

questions.question: Summative assessment is mainly used to:
options: Judge achievement at the end of a unit or course
questions.explanation: Summative assessment evaluates learning at the conclusion of a defined instructional period.

questions.question: Assessment for learning is most closely associated with:
options: Feedback that helps improve ongoing learning
questions.explanation: Assessment for learning uses evidence and feedback to move learning forward.

questions.question: A test gives consistent results under similar conditions. This property is:
questions.explanation: Reliability concerns consistency of measurement.

questions.question: A test measures the learning outcome it is intended to measure. This concerns:
questions.explanation: Validity concerns whether evidence supports the intended interpretation and use of scores.

questions.question: Which practice supports inclusive education?
options: Keeping learners with disabilities out of ordinary activities
Providing reasonable accommodations and meaningful participation
Using one rigid method for everyone
questions.explanation: Inclusive education removes barriers and supports participation and learning for all students.

questions.question: Universal Design for Learning encourages teachers to provide multiple means of:
options: Engagement, representation, and action or expression
questions.explanation: UDL plans flexible options for engagement, representation, and action and expression.

questions.question: A learner has difficulty reading printed text. Which adjustment may improve access?
options: Offer accessible digital text or audio when appropriate
Exclude the learner from reading tasks
questions.explanation: Accessible formats can reduce barriers while keeping the learner connected to meaningful goals.

questions.question: Differentiated instruction means:
options: Giving every learner exactly the same support regardless of need
Adjusting content, process or product in response to readiness and needs
Removing challenging content from all lessons
questions.explanation: Differentiation varies aspects of instruction to address learner readiness, interests and profiles.

questions.question: Which is a useful response to a persistent misconception?
options: Ignore it to finish the syllabus
Elicit the learner’s reasoning and use targeted feedback or examples
questions.explanation: Understanding the reasoning behind an error helps the teacher plan useful feedback and instruction.

questions.question: Metacognition involves:
options: Thinking about and regulating one’s own thinking
questions.explanation: Metacognition includes monitoring and regulating one’s cognitive processes.

questions.question: Which learner behaviour shows self-regulated learning?
options: Setting a goal, monitoring progress and changing strategy when needed
Waiting for every instruction without reflection
questions.explanation: Self-regulated learners plan, monitor and evaluate their learning and adjust strategies.

questions.question: A teacher asks learners to explain how they reached an answer. This can help reveal:
questions.explanation: Explaining reasoning provides evidence about thinking, strategies and misunderstandings.

questions.question: Which classroom question is most open-ended?
options: What different methods could solve this problem, and why?
questions.explanation: Open-ended questions allow a range of reasoned responses rather than a single yes/no answer.

questions.question: A teacher connects a new concept to learners’ everyday experiences. This supports:
questions.explanation: Connecting new ideas with prior knowledge and experience can support understanding.

questions.question: Prior knowledge is important because it:
options: Can shape how learners interpret new information
questions.explanation: Learners use existing knowledge to interpret new concepts, although misconceptions may also influence learning.

questions.question: Which is a characteristic of cooperative learning?
options: Learners work together toward shared goals with individual accountability
One learner completes all tasks for everyone
questions.explanation: Cooperative learning combines collaboration with structures that support each learner’s contribution.

questions.question: Peer assessment is most productive when learners:
options: Use clear criteria and constructive feedback
Assign grades without understanding the task
questions.explanation: Clear criteria and constructive comments make peer assessment more useful and fair.

questions.question: Which feedback is most actionable?
options: Your evidence is relevant; add an explanation linking it to your claim
questions.explanation: Specific feedback identifies what is working and what concrete next step can improve the work.

questions.question: A teacher uses a rubric before a project begins. This helps learners understand:
options: The criteria and expectations for quality
That all projects must be identical
questions.explanation: Sharing a rubric clarifies expectations and supports planning and self-assessment.

questions.question: Which approach is most consistent with a growth mindset?
options: Abilities can develop through effective strategies, effort and support
Mistakes prove a learner cannot improve
questions.explanation: A growth mindset emphasises development through learning, strategies, effort and support.

questions.question: A learner’s repeated failure may be affected by:
options: Instructional, environmental, emotional and individual factors
Nothing that a teacher can investigate
questions.explanation: Learning outcomes can reflect interacting factors, so teachers should investigate rather than assume one cause.

questions.question: Which is an example of a protective classroom climate?
options: Respectful relationships and predictable, fair expectations
questions.explanation: A supportive climate combines respect, safety and consistent expectations.

questions.question: A teacher notices a sudden change in a learner’s participation. An appropriate first step is to:
options: Observe, speak privately and sensitively, and follow school support procedures
Announce the concern to the class
Punish the learner for being quiet
questions.explanation: A sensitive conversation and appropriate school procedures help identify support without making assumptions.

questions.question: Guidance in schools generally aims to:
options: Help learners understand themselves and make informed choices
questions.explanation: Guidance supports personal, educational and career development and informed decision-making.

questions.question: Counselling differs from ordinary advice-giving because it typically involves:
options: A purposeful helping relationship and attentive exploration
questions.explanation: Counselling uses a structured, supportive relationship to help a person explore concerns and options.

questions.question: Confidentiality in school counselling should be understood as:
options: Important, while recognising safeguarding and legal limits
A reason to avoid recordkeeping policies
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is important, but concerns involving safety or legal duties may require appropriate disclosure under policy.

questions.question: Which response is appropriate when a learner discloses possible abuse?
options: Listen calmly, avoid leading questions, and follow safeguarding/reporting procedures
Promise to keep it secret no matter what
questions.explanation: The adult should respond supportively, avoid investigating beyond their role, and follow safeguarding requirements.

questions.question: Which is a reasonable classroom management strategy?
options: Teach routines explicitly and reinforce them consistently
questions.explanation: Clear routines, explicit expectations and consistent responses support an orderly learning environment.

questions.question: A restorative approach after conflict focuses on:
options: Understanding harm, responsibility and repairing relationships
questions.explanation: Restorative practices seek accountability, repair and safer relationships.

questions.question: Which practice can reduce stereotype threat in the classroom?
options: Communicate high expectations with belonging, fair treatment and supportive feedback
questions.explanation: Supportive, inclusive conditions can help reduce cues that learners are judged through stereotypes.

questions.question: Gender-responsive teaching should:
options: Challenge limiting stereotypes and provide equitable participation
Assume all boys or girls learn identically
questions.explanation: Equitable teaching challenges stereotypes and notices whether opportunities and participation are fair.

questions.question: Which statement about intelligence is most defensible?
options: A single test captures every aspect of a person’s potential
Performance can be influenced by many abilities and contextual factors
One score should determine a learner’s future
questions.explanation: Human abilities are multifaceted, and test scores provide limited evidence shaped by context and measurement.

questions.question: A teacher uses examples, diagrams and a short discussion to introduce a concept. This provides:
options: Varied representations and routes into the content
Evidence that learners have one fixed learning style
questions.explanation: Different representations can make concepts accessible; this does not mean learners must be assigned fixed learning-style labels.

questions.question: Which is a sound use of grouping?
options: Use flexible groups that change with task and evidence of need
Keep learners permanently ranked by one test
Prevent learners from working with others
questions.explanation: Flexible grouping allows support and collaboration to respond to changing learning goals and evidence.

questions.question: A curriculum is aligned when:
options: Objectives, learning activities and assessment support one another
questions.explanation: Constructive alignment connects intended outcomes, teaching-learning activities and assessment.

questions.question: Which objective is most measurable?
options: Compare two fractions and justify which is larger
questions.explanation: A measurable objective states an observable performance and the expected task.

questions.question: A teacher begins a lesson with a short question to identify what learners already know. This is:
questions.explanation: Diagnostic assessment helps identify prior knowledge, readiness or learning needs before instruction.

questions.question: Which evidence best supports a claim that a learner has mastered a skill?
options: Repeated performance on relevant tasks using clear criteria
questions.explanation: Mastery judgments should be based on relevant evidence and transparent criteria, ideally across opportunities.

questions.question: Which is an example of transfer of learning?
options: Applying a mathematical strategy to a new but related problem
Repeating a definition only in the same wording
Copying a worked answer without understanding
questions.explanation: Transfer occurs when learning is applied in a different or novel situation.

questions.question: In constructivist teaching, learners are viewed as:
options: Active participants who build and revise understanding
Empty containers who only receive facts
questions.explanation: Constructivist approaches emphasise learners’ active construction of meaning through experience and reflection.

questions.question: Which practice helps make classroom discussion inclusive?
options: Set norms, allow thinking time and invite varied ways to contribute
Require every response to be spoken publicly
questions.explanation: Multiple participation routes, wait time and respectful norms broaden access to discussion.

questions.question: Wait time after asking a question can:
options: Give learners time to think and formulate responses
questions.explanation: Adequate wait time can support more considered responses and wider participation.

questions.question: Which is a useful way to respond to an incorrect answer?
options: Ask the learner to explain their thinking and guide them toward revision
Assume the learner did not study
questions.explanation: Exploring the reasoning behind an error helps turn it into a learning opportunity.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a learning disability?
options: A specific difficulty that may affect particular academic skills and requires appropriate assessment and support
A condition that makes all learning impossible
Something diagnosed solely from one classroom mistake
questions.explanation: Learning disabilities involve specific learning difficulties and should be assessed appropriately, with suitable support.

questions.question: An accommodation generally changes:
options: How a learner accesses or demonstrates learning, without necessarily changing the learning standard
questions.explanation: Accommodations address access or response barriers while preserving the intended learning expectation when appropriate.

questions.question: A modification generally refers to:
options: A change to what a learner is expected to learn or demonstrate
A different font with identical expectations
Extra wait time in all cases
questions.explanation: Modifications alter learning expectations or content, unlike accommodations that primarily change access or response.

questions.question: Which is an example of assistive technology?
options: A screen reader that reads digital text aloud
questions.explanation: A screen reader is technology that can improve access to digital information for users who need it.

questions.question: Which action supports learners who are multilingual?
options: Use visuals, clarify key vocabulary and connect with existing language resources
Treat home languages as evidence of low ability
Assess subject knowledge only through unfamiliar idioms
questions.explanation: Language scaffolds can support access to subject learning while valuing learners’ linguistic resources.

questions.question: Which statement about bilingualism is appropriate?
options: Knowing more than one language inherently prevents conceptual learning
Learners can draw on language resources as they develop academic proficiency
Home language should always be ignored
Language proficiency and subject knowledge are exactly the same
questions.explanation: Multilingual learners may use their language resources to make meaning; language proficiency should not be confused with subject understanding.

questions.question: A teacher adapts an activity after reviewing exit-ticket responses. This demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Responsive instruction uses evidence of learning to decide what to reteach, extend or change.

questions.question: Which is a suitable purpose for an exit ticket?
options: Gather brief evidence of understanding at the end of a lesson
Replace all assessments for the year
questions.explanation: Exit tickets provide a quick snapshot of learners’ understanding and questions.

questions.question: A portfolio is useful because it can show:
options: Growth and examples of work over time
questions.explanation: A portfolio can document progress, reflection and achievement across multiple pieces of work.

questions.question: Which is a feature of authentic assessment?
options: Learners apply knowledge or skills in meaningful tasks
Every task is unrelated to real use
questions.explanation: Authentic assessment asks learners to use knowledge and skills in meaningful contexts.

questions.question: Which is an example of criterion-referenced interpretation?
options: Comparing performance with stated standards or criteria
Comparing each learner only with the class rank
questions.explanation: Criterion-referenced interpretation describes performance against defined expectations.

questions.question: Norm-referenced interpretation compares a learner’s performance with:
options: The performance of a reference group
questions.explanation: Norm-referenced scores indicate standing relative to a specified comparison group.

questions.question: Which factor can threaten assessment fairness?
options: Irrelevant language complexity in a test intended to measure another skill
questions.explanation: Construct-irrelevant barriers, such as unnecessary language demands, can distort what a test measures.

questions.question: A teacher reviews which distractors many learners selected on an MCQ. This can help identify:
questions.explanation: Distractor patterns can reveal misunderstandings and may also signal an item that needs review.

questions.question: Which statement about feedback timing is reasonable?
options: Feedback should be timely enough to inform the next learning steps
Feedback is useful only months later
Immediate feedback is always best for every task
questions.explanation: Feedback is most useful when learners can understand and use it; timing depends on the task and purpose.

questions.question: Which practice supports academic integrity while teaching research skills?
options: Teach attribution, note-taking and responsible use of sources
questions.explanation: Explicit instruction in attribution and source use helps learners complete work responsibly.

questions.question: A teacher wants to encourage deeper thinking. Which prompt is suitable?
options: Why might this solution work, and what evidence supports it?
questions.explanation: Asking for reasons and evidence encourages analysis and justification.

questions.question: Which task primarily involves analysis?
options: Separate an argument into claims and evidence and examine their relationships
questions.explanation: Analysis involves examining components and relationships, such as how evidence supports claims.

questions.question: Which task primarily involves evaluation?
options: Judge two solutions against explicit criteria and justify the judgment
questions.explanation: Evaluation requires making and justifying judgments using criteria.

questions.question: Which task primarily involves creation?
options: Design and present a solution to a defined problem
questions.explanation: Creation involves putting elements together to produce a new or original product or solution.

questions.question: A teacher uses a concept map to help learners organise ideas. This mainly supports:
questions.explanation: Concept maps represent links among ideas and can support organisation and review.

questions.question: Retrieval practice involves:
options: Rereading passively without trying to recall
Copying answers while looking at them
questions.explanation: Retrieval practice strengthens access to learned information by requiring recall.

questions.question: Spaced practice means:
options: Distributing study or practice across time
Doing all practice in one uninterrupted session
questions.explanation: Spacing spreads practice over time rather than concentrating it into one massed session.

questions.question: Interleaving practice involves:
options: Mixing related problem types or topics during practice
questions.explanation: Interleaving requires learners to distinguish among different kinds of problems or concepts.

questions.question: Which is an example of elaboration?
options: Explain why a concept is true and connect it to another idea
Copy the same sentence repeatedly without thought
questions.explanation: Elaboration builds meaningful links by explaining and connecting ideas.

questions.question: Which condition is most supportive of attention during instruction?
options: Clear goals, manageable segments and purposeful learner activity
questions.explanation: Organised instruction and purposeful activity can help learners direct attention to relevant information.

questions.question: Which is a responsible way to use educational technology?
options: Choose tools based on learning goals, access, privacy and effectiveness
Use technology only because it is new
questions.explanation: Technology choices should serve learning and account for accessibility, privacy and practical constraints.

questions.question: A teacher uses a simulation to explore a difficult-to-observe process. The simulation is useful when it:
options: Helps learners investigate a model while recognising its limitations
Is treated as identical to reality in every detail
Removes the need for learning goals
questions.explanation: Simulations can make processes available for exploration, but learners should understand that models have limitations.

questions.question: Which is an example of experiential learning?
options: Learners conduct an activity, reflect on it and apply what they learned
Learners receive marks without doing a task
questions.explanation: Experiential learning connects experience with reflection and subsequent application.

questions.question: Which role should a teacher take when facilitating inquiry?
options: Support questioning, evidence gathering and reflection
questions.explanation: Inquiry facilitation helps learners ask questions, examine evidence and reflect on conclusions.

questions.question: A learner proposes a hypothesis. What should follow in a sound inquiry process?
options: Identify evidence or a procedure that could test it
questions.explanation: A hypothesis should be examined through relevant evidence or testing.

questions.question: Which is a useful way to build classroom belonging?
options: Learn and pronounce names respectfully and establish inclusive norms
questions.explanation: Respectful recognition and inclusive norms can help learners feel accepted and participate.

questions.question: A teacher suspects a learner is experiencing bullying. The teacher should:
options: Take the concern seriously, ensure safety and follow school procedures
Tell the learner to tolerate it
Publicly confront the alleged students without preparation
questions.explanation: Bullying concerns require a safe, timely response consistent with school safeguarding and reporting procedures.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects a trauma-informed approach?
options: Prioritise safety, predictability, trust and supportive relationships
Assume every behaviour is deliberate defiance
questions.explanation: Trauma-informed practice emphasises safety and supportive, predictable interactions without requiring disclosure.

questions.question: Which is a professional boundary for a teacher?
options: Maintain respectful relationships and use approved communication channels
Use learners to meet personal needs
questions.explanation: Professional boundaries protect learners and maintain appropriate teacher-student relationships.

questions.question: Which action supports collaboration with families?
options: Communicate respectfully, share specific learning information and listen to family perspectives
Contact families only to blame them
Assume every family has identical resources
questions.explanation: Two-way, respectful communication can support a shared understanding of a learner’s progress and needs.

questions.question: Which approach is appropriate when family participation is limited by work schedules or language?
options: Offer accessible communication options and flexible opportunities where possible
Conclude that the family does not care
questions.explanation: Flexible and accessible options can reduce barriers to family-school communication.

questions.question: Which statement about child development is most accurate?
options: Development includes physical, cognitive, social and emotional dimensions that interact
questions.explanation: Development is multidimensional, and changes in one domain can relate to changes in others.

questions.question: The principle of continuity in development means that:
options: Development is a gradual process, though its pace and pattern may vary
Every skill appears suddenly at the same age
questions.explanation: Development generally unfolds over time, with variation in rate and sequence among individuals.

questions.question: The principle of individual variation means teachers should:
options: Avoid assuming every learner reaches milestones at exactly the same time
Use age as the only measure of ability
questions.explanation: Learners vary in pace and patterns, so instruction should respond to evidence about individual needs.
